title: A Prophet's Rebuke and Jehoshaphat's Reform of Justice
summary: Back from the battle where Ahab died, Jehoshaphat is confronted by the seer Jehu son of Hanani: he has helped the wicked and loved those who hate the LORD, and wrath is upon him, yet some good is found in him. Jehoshaphat responds by traveling through his kingdom to turn the people back to the LORD, appointing judges in the fortified cities, and setting up a court in Jerusalem of Levites, priests, and family heads, charging all of them to judge in the fear of the LORD.
story: Chapter 18 ended with Jehoshaphat narrowly escaping death in Ahab's war. This short chapter shows how he responded to that experience and to prophetic correction. Unlike his father Asa, who jailed the seer Hanani (16:10), Jehoshaphat accepts the rebuke of Hanani's son and turns it into reform. The chapter's attention to justice fits his name, which means the LORD judges. The next chapter will put his renewed faith to the test when a great coalition invades Judah.
historical:
Jehu son of Hanani belonged to a family of prophets. His father Hanani had rebuked Asa (16:7), and Jehu himself had earlier pronounced judgment on Baasha of Israel (1 Kings 16:1-7); 20:34 says he also wrote an account of Jehoshaphat's reign. The judicial reform of verses 4 to 11 appears only in Chronicles. Scholars debate how much of it reflects Jehoshaphat's own time and how much reflects institutions familiar in the Chronicler's day; some argue that a royal organization of justice in the ninth century is entirely plausible, while others see later patterns in the details. The text itself presents it as Jehoshaphat's work.

The reform reached from Beersheba in the far south to the hill country of Ephraim in the north, the full extent of his territory, including the northern towns taken by Asa. Amariah the chief priest and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, are otherwise little known; the division between matters of the LORD and matters of the king shows a separation between religious and royal cases in the highest court.
cultural:
In ancient Israel, justice was ordinarily administered by the elders of each town sitting at the city gate. Deuteronomy commanded that judges and officials be appointed in every town (Deuteronomy 16:18-20) and that hard cases be brought to the priests and the judge at the central sanctuary (Deuteronomy 17:8-13). Jehoshaphat's arrangement follows that pattern: local judges in the fortified cities and a higher court in Jerusalem. The categories in verse 10 (bloodshed, and questions of law, commandment, statutes, and ordinances) cover both criminal cases and disputes over the meaning of God's law.

Bribery and partiality were the great corruptions of ancient justice, as they are of modern justice. The law repeatedly forbade taking bribes and showing favoritism to rich or poor (Exodus 23:6-8; Leviticus 19:15). Jehoshaphat grounds the prohibition in the character of God: with the LORD there is no injustice, partiality, or bribery, so those who judge on his behalf must be the same.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 3 are a prophetic oracle of judgment with a note of mercy, following the pattern of rebuke and assessment used elsewhere in Chronicles. Verses 4 to 11 contain two royal speeches, one to the local judges (verses 6 and 7) and one to the Jerusalem court (verses 9 to 11). Both speeches repeat the same key ideas: the fear of the LORD, care in what one does, faithfulness, and the presence of the LORD with those who judge. The chapter uses the root for judging repeatedly, which echoes the king's own name. The final words, "may the LORD be with the upright", end on blessing rather than warning.

outline.t: Jehu son of Hanani rebukes Jehoshaphat
Jehoshaphat turns the people to the LORD and appoints local judges
The court in Jerusalem and the king's charge to it

doctrines.note: Verse 7 grounds human justice in God's own character: with the LORD there is no injustice, partiality, or bribery. Judges act on his behalf, so they must reflect who he is.
The reform brings God's law into daily life through local courts. The law is not only for worship but also for settling disputes, protecting life, and warning people before they incur guilt.
Jehoshaphat responds to rebuke by turning the people back to the LORD. Prophetic correction received well leads to renewal rather than to resentment.

words.note: Shaphat, to judge, govern, or vindicate. The verb forms part of Jehoshaphat's name, which means the LORD judges. In the Old Testament judging includes deciding cases and also rescuing the wronged, so good judges both punish wrongdoers and protect the vulnerable.

Shochad, a bribe or gift given to influence judgment. The law says a bribe blinds the clear-sighted (Exodus 23:8). Jehoshaphat says there is no bribery with the LORD, so there must be none among his judges.

Yir'ah, fear or reverence. The fear of the LORD is the Old Testament's name for a life lived in reverent awareness of God. For judges, it means remembering that God is present in the court and sees what they do.
Emunah, faithfulness or steadiness, related to amen. The Jerusalem judges are charged to serve faithfully and wholeheartedly. It describes reliability, the quality of someone who can be trusted.

christ: Jehoshaphat's charge to his judges reflects the hope for a king who would establish justice, a hope stated in passages such as Isaiah 11:3-5, which describes a shoot from Jesse's line who will judge the poor with righteousness and not by what his eyes see. The New Testament presents Jesus as that king and as the one to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22), a judge without partiality (Acts 10:34, 42). Jehu's rebuke about loving those who hate the LORD also raises a question the gospel reframes: Jesus calls his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44), which is different from making political alliances that draw one into another's sin. The links here are thematic.

hard.q: Jehu asks whether Jehoshaphat should love those who hate the LORD. Doesn't Jesus command love for enemies?
hard.a: Jehu's rebuke concerns a specific political and military alliance. Jehoshaphat had joined his house to Ahab's by marriage and fought Ahab's war, lending his strength to a king who promoted Baal worship. In Hebrew covenant language, to love can mean to be loyal to or to ally with, as in treaty relationships. The rebuke is about entering a partnership that supported the enemies of God and drew Judah into their idolatry, which the next chapters show happened through the marriage of Jehoram and Athaliah. Jesus' command to love enemies calls for goodwill, prayer, and kindness toward those who oppose us. The two teachings address different things: one forbids yoking oneself to another's evil, and the other forbids hatred and revenge. Christians have often found in passages like 2 Corinthians 6:14 a New Testament parallel to Jehu's warning.

questions: Jehu told Jehoshaphat both that wrath was upon him and that some good was found in him. Why is it important to hear both parts of an honest assessment?
Jehoshaphat told his judges they judged for the LORD, not for man. How would it change your work if you saw it as done before God?
The chapter treats bribery and partiality as betrayals of God's character. Where are you tempted to favor people who can benefit you?
